title: A New Clock Uses the Centers of Atoms to Keep Time
summary:
Scientists in Vienna, Austria, have built the world's first self-stabilizing nuclear clock. One day, it could keep time even better than today's best atomic clocks.

Atomic clocks use electrons, tiny particles that move around the center of an atom. The new clock uses the nucleus, which is the atom's center. The nucleus is much less bothered by things around it.

The clock uses an element called thorium. Scientists can use laser light to switch thorium's nucleus between two energy states.

In the new clock, a laser shines on a crystal that contains thorium. The laser's light vibrates with a steady rhythm that can measure time. But the rhythm can drift, for example when the temperature changes. The thorium only soaks up the light when it is exactly right. If the laser drifts, the clock notices and fixes it by itself.

The team showed the clock could run steadily for more than 24 hours without help.
why_it_matters: Super-exact clocks help scientists measure things very carefully, which can lead to new discoveries and better technology kids use.

background_read: Everything is made of tiny atoms, and each atom has a center called a nucleus.
The best clocks today, called atomic clocks, use the tiny vibrations of atoms to keep very exact time.
Scientists want even better clocks so they can measure things more precisely.

WHY: Using the nucleus of an atom could make clocks even more exact than atomic clocks
